name: Gloo: AI Products and Research for Churches and Faith Organisations
title: Gloo: AI Products and Research for Churches and Faith Organisations
answer: Gloo is a technology platform used by churches that publishes AI products and research on AI in ministry. Its most useful contribution is a Barna study for its State of the Church series finding that 94% of pastors and 83% of practising Christians worry about AI misinterpreting scripture, the highest concern Barna recorded in any group surveyed, alongside its Flourishing AI benchmark, in which none of 24 tested AI models passed.

sections.body: Gloo publishes this material on gloo.us across product and research pages. The product page describes AI offerings for developers, enterprises and churches. Two research pages carry findings: a Barna study for Gloo's State of the Church series on AI and Bible interpretation, and the Flourishing AI Initiative's FAI-C Insights Report, published on June 22, 2026. The material is Gloo's own, combining survey research with benchmark testing of AI models.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: Gloo frames AI as a foundational capability across its platform, intended to support mission effectiveness, preserve relational ministry and create practical value across what it calls the faith and flourishing ecosystem. Executive Chairman Pat Gelsinger says the aim is trusted, open, useful AI that humanity can build on, and CEO Scott Beck says AI should enable rather than replace relationships. The offer covers trust infrastructure, AI solutions that deliver work, and organisational onboarding and transformation, with Gloo AI Studio and the YouVersion developer platform giving builders backend tools. The Barna study for the State of the Church series reports that 94% of pastors and 83% of practising Christians are concerned about AI misinterpreting scripture, the highest concern among any group Barna surveyed. Only one in ten pastors wants AI to name the correct interpretation of a hard passage, while practising Christians are 2.5 times as likely to want the right answer from AI. Just 5% of pastors say AI should not answer questions about contested passages, and 9% say it should not interpret theology where scholars disagree. 60% of pastors prefer AI to present multiple theological viewpoints side by side with scholarly citations to encourage critical thinking, and pastors generally treat AI as an aid to personal study rather than an authoritative source. The Flourishing AI Initiative's benchmark evaluates how well AI models support human flourishing, finding that current models systematically underperform in dimensions critical to spiritual and existential well-being, with the Faith dimension consistently scoring lowest. Gloo attributes this to models defaulting to secular or neutral responses, avoiding explicit Christian claims and struggling with the theological grounding the rubric requires. None of the 24 AI models tested passed.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source gives 94% of pastors and 83% of practising Christians concerned about AI misinterpreting scripture; one in ten pastors wanting AI to name the correct interpretation of a hard passage; practising Christians 2.5 times as likely to want the right answer from AI; 5% of pastors saying AI should not answer questions on contested passages; 9% saying it should not interpret theology where scholars disagree; 60% of pastors preferring multiple viewpoints with scholarly citations; more than 600 participants in Gloo's hackathon; 24 AI models tested with none passing the FAI-C benchmark; and a report date of June 22, 2026.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For anyone following AI in congregations, this source supplies both deployment detail and demand-side evidence. The product pages show what a sector platform actually builds, from trust infrastructure to developer tools shared with YouVersion, and the hackathon indicates an active builder community. The Barna findings give a rare measure of what pastors and practising Christians want from AI in interpretation, showing a preference for multiple cited viewpoints over single answers. The FAI-C benchmark adds a testing result, that the Faith dimension scores lowest and no tested model passed, which is directly relevant to anyone selecting or evaluating models for ministry use.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Churches and Faith Organisations

sections.body: The material is published by Gloo about Gloo's own products and research, so the product claims are promotional in nature and the benchmark is the initiative's own. The Barna study is reported through Gloo's summary rather than in full, so sampling and methodology are not given here. The pages cover Bible interpretation and flourishing metrics but not other ministry applications, and the FAI-C report is dated June 22, 2026, so its model results reflect that point in time.
